title: WY, O. WY?: Why America’s state abbreviations make no sense - The Tartan
content: The United States Postal Service (USPS) offers Americans many things, such as reliable shipping, sustainability initiatives, and digital tracking. However, these accomplishments do not erase its biggest mistake: the state abbreviations. In the 1800s, Americans started abbreviating everything — s.p. meant “small potatoes,” n.g. meant “no go,” and the popular phrase “OK” became okay to use after Charles Gordon Greene, editor of the Boston Morning Post, used it in 1839. To accommodate Americans’ desire to avoid writing full words, in 1831,  the USPS released its first list of state abbreviations. The original list followed a simple pattern: use the first and last letter of the state (VA for Virginia, PA for Pennsylvania). With only 28 states at the time, avoiding duplicates was easy. Yet the USPS immediately ignored its own logic. Arkansas was abbreviated to Ar. T. — an interesting choice since the only other “A” state was Alabama (AL), leaving zero risk of confusion. Where did the “T” even come from? It gets worse. Ohio, a state with a rapidly growing population in the 1830s, was abbreviated as just “O.” Yup. As in, “‘O’ my goodness, that is a terrible choice.” In 1874, the USPS updated the list for new states, creating the most sensible list yet. Abbreviations could be long enough to preserve characteristic sounds. Arizona became Ariz. to avoid clashing with Arkansas (Ark.), while Massachusetts, Minnesota, and Mississippi became Mass., Minn., and Miss. By 1943, the last of the U.S. states were added using this clear, phonetic approach. Everything fell apart in 1963 when the USPS introduced the Zone Improvement Plan (ZIP). ZIP streamlined sorting, but scanning technology capped the bottom address line at 23 characters (including spaces), making the longer phonetic names of the Practical Era unusable. In June 1963, abbreviations ranged from two to five capital letters. By Oct. 1963, the USPS standardized every state to the exact two-letter uppercase system we have today. This is where USPS’s thought process unravels. Both Washington and Wisconsin begin with “W” and end with “N,” so neither of them gets WN. Defaulting to their first two letters (WA and WI) makes sense. But why did Wyoming become WY? No other state starts with “W” and ends with “G.” Why abandon Rule One when there’s zero conflict? We see this same mistake with Utah (UT). It is the only state that starts with “U.” Wouldn’t UH follow the rule? Again, Ohio, Oklahoma, and Oregon should be OO, OA, and ON. Instead, we get OH, OK, and OR. If you assume they wanted one vowel and one consonant, I present Texas (TX) and Tennessee (TN). Both could use Rule One without conflict, yet both combine two consonants. If WN is banned because of Wisconsin and Washington, and NA is banned because of Nebraska and Nevada … Why is Iowa shortened to IA when that could be Indiana? It doesn’t make sense! Florida is FL (instead of FA), even though it is the only “F” state. Yet Georgia (GA) and Hawaii (HI) — also sole owners of their starting letters — follow Rule One. Why use MA (which could be confused with Maine or Maryland) for Massachusetts instead of MS, when it is the only state starting with “M” and ending with “S”? I’m sure that everyone knows their home state’s abbreviation. Residents in my home state, Virginia — one of the rare states that actually follows the rules — use its abbreviation casually. “I’m from NoVA (Northern Virginia),” hundreds of Carnegie Mellon students say. “Oh cool, I love going to VA,” no one has ever said. This sensible abbreviation allows it to seamlessly fit into conversation, but I doubt anyone in Nebraska has declared, “I am so proud of NE’s commitment to wildlife conservation!” On the surface, chaotic abbreviations are a minor quirk of American postal history. But on a deeper level, they highlight a classic bureaucratic paradox: the government creates a rigid system for efficiency, only to abandon its own logic at every turn. We accept this nonsensical code without a second thought — writing MO for Missouri as if there is any justification for that abbreviation. This is my application to re-abbreviate every state, but also my invitation to question arbitrary rules we follow every day. If the government expects us to fall in line, the least they can do is follow their own principles. I’m a second year undergraduate in the Mechanical Engineering department.

title: What Could Stall AbbVie Stock’s Run? - Trefis
content: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com. AbbVie (ABBV) stock returned 38.4% over the past twelve months, compared with a 9.8% return for the S&P 500. The shares closed on November 6 just 1.2% below their high for the year. Following a run like that, shareholders want to know what might slow the stock down. Management pointed to a specific headwind during the company’s October 30 earnings call, naming a pressure that begins in 2027. What is that pressure, and has AbbVie felt it before? During the fiscal Q3 2026 call, management said the IRA price for the psychiatry drug Vraylar will begin in 2027, and instructed analysts to build it into their models. Under a U.S. drug-pricing law known as the IRA, the government can select certain drugs and publish prices for them. Management did not specify on the call how much of Vraylar’s sales will face that price impact. AbbVie has encountered this before. Sales of the cancer drug Imbruvica fell 26.1% in fiscal Q3 2026, a decline management attributed to IRA pricing and competitive share pressure. Imbruvica’s revenue had already dropped 6.9% in fiscal 2024 and 14.3% in fiscal 2025. Vraylar is the next AbbVie drug management has named, even as it continues to grow. Global sales of the treatment reached nearly $1.1 billion in fiscal Q3 2026, marking an increase of 14.3%. In fiscal 2025, Vraylar sales rose 10.8% from a year earlier to $3.62 billion. That performance accounted for 5.9% of the company’s revenue for the year. Management expects the drug to reach $4.2 billion in sales for fiscal 2026, so the drug is still adding sales right up to the year its price begins. Botox remains an open question. Sales of Botox Therapeutic climbed 14.8% to $3.77 billion in fiscal 2025, making it slightly larger than Vraylar. During the call, management argued the IRA cannot select Botox because human serum albumin, one of its three ingredients, derives from human blood plasma. A federal district court ruled in AbbVie’s favor on that point the day before the call. The company added that the matter is not over since the government can still appeal, and management noted it does not expect a price to be published while that plays out. Investors are currently paying a high price for AbbVie’s earnings. The stock trades at 49.8 times its last twelve months of earnings, compared with 21.8 for the S&P 500. That valuation relies on reported earnings, which run well below the company’s adjusted measure. During fiscal Q3 2026, AbbVie recorded $2.37 a share under its reported measure, alongside an adjusted figure of $3.82 a share. While the IRA price presents a real cost, it has reached AbbVie one drug at a time so far, and the company has kept growing through the first one. Total revenue rose 10.3% in fiscal Q3 2026, even as Imbruvica’s sales shrank. Management said that many sell-side models already appear to include the Vraylar price, and the company expects top-tier growth again in 2027. AbbVie stock has also fallen less than the S&P 500 during most recent market shocks. The shares dropped 13.0% in the 2025 tariff shock, compared with a 19.0% decline for the index. During the 2022 inflation shock, the stock shed 1.5%, while the index fell 24.0%. The 2023 banking crisis stood as an exception, with AbbVie falling 13.0% as the S&P 500 fell 6.7%. Holding up in a shock is a portfolio’s job too. Here’s how to set one up for a crash and a rally. For the risk to be worth taking, AbbVie’s growing drugs must continue adding more in sales than Vraylar gives up once its price begins. The company’s two largest drugs, Skyrizi and Rinvoq, brought in $17.6 billion and $8.3 billion in fiscal 2025, reflecting increases of 49.9% and 39.1%. Vraylar’s sales, alongside the 2027 guidance management plans to deliver during the fourth-quarter call, are the figures to watch when AbbVie reports in February 2027.
